title: Syntax
summary: Learn the small pieces every Java program needs before it can run.
refresher: Java is picky about shape. A basic program lives inside a **class**, starts running at **main**, and uses **braces** to group code. **Semicolons** end most statements. If one of those pieces is missing, the compiler usually stops before the program ever runs.

output-01.title: Numbers add before they print
output-01.body: This checks whether the values are numbers or text. Number values use `+` for arithmetic before output happens.
output-01.notice: Evaluate the expression first, then decide what the output instruction shows.
output-01.mistake: Do not join digits like text unless quotes make them strings.

output-02.title: A variable name stands in for its value
output-02.body: The output line uses the stored value, not the variable name as literal text.
output-02.notice: Read the assignment first so the later output line has the value in place.
output-02.mistake: Do not choose an answer that prints the name itself when the code uses the variable.

output-03.title: Text plus text joins
output-03.body: When both sides are strings, `+` makes one longer string instead of doing arithmetic.
output-03.notice: Quotes are the clue that the values are text.
output-03.mistake: Do not add quoted digits as numbers unless the code converts them first.

output-04.title: Integer division keeps a whole result
output-04.body: This question tests the division rule for whole-number output in the selected language.
output-04.notice: Check whether the code asks for decimal division or a whole-number result.
output-04.mistake: Do not round up. Whole-number division keeps the complete groups.

output-05.title: Printing needs the exact output call
output-05.body: Type-in output questions care about the statement shape and the exact text being shown.
output-05.notice: Match the print/output function and include quotes around text.
output-05.mistake: Do not type only the word being printed when the question asks for a statement.

syntax-delimiter-01.title: Open delimiters need partners
syntax-delimiter-01.body: Brackets, parentheses, and quotes create a shape the parser must be able to close.
syntax-delimiter-01.notice: When code stops before running, scan for the opening symbol that never got closed.
syntax-delimiter-01.mistake: Do not debug the logic until the code can be parsed.

syntax-comment-01.title: Comments are skipped
syntax-comment-01.body: A comment can look like code, but the language ignores it when the program runs.
syntax-comment-01.notice: Only non-commented output statements affect what appears.
syntax-comment-01.mistake: Do not count a commented-out line as a printed line.

syntax-case-01.title: Names are case-sensitive
syntax-case-01.body: Capitalization can create a different name. Built-in words and user names must match exactly.
syntax-case-01.notice: If a familiar name fails, compare every letter including case.
syntax-case-01.mistake: Do not assume `Print` and `print` are the same spelling to the language.

syntax-line-break-01.title: Escapes can create invisible characters
syntax-line-break-01.body: Some characters inside strings describe formatting, such as moving output to the next line.
syntax-line-break-01.notice: Read escape sequences as one special character, not as ordinary letters.
syntax-line-break-01.mistake: Do not include the backslash text literally when the code asks for output.

syntax-block-01.title: Block headers need block syntax
syntax-block-01.body: A decision or loop header must clearly mark that a controlled body is coming next.
syntax-block-01.notice: Check the small symbol at the end of the header and the shape of the body below it.
syntax-block-01.mistake: Do not focus only on the condition and miss the punctuation that opens the block.

sections.title: Class, main, and the file name
sections.summary: Start with the outer **program shape** Java expects before any line can run.

blocks.body: Java asks for more structure than Python. Even a tiny program sits inside a **class**, and the first code that runs goes inside a **method** named `main`. At first, that wrapper may feel like extra typing. Think of it as the envelope Java needs before it can read your message.

blocks.caption: The **class** is the outside box. **main** is where Java starts. The **print** line is the one instruction we wrote.

blocks.body: **Braces** mark where a block starts and ends. The **class** has its own pair. main has its own pair inside the class. Most beginner **syntax errors** come from losing one brace, one quote, or one semicolon.

blocks.title: The file name has to match the class name
blocks.body: If a Java **class** is marked `public`, the **file** name must match that class name exactly. `public class Hello` belongs in `Hello.java`. A mismatch stops the program before it runs.

sections.title: Statements and semicolons
sections.summary: Use **semicolons** to show Java where one instruction ends and the next begins.

blocks.body: Inside main, you write statements. A **statement** is one instruction, and it ends with a **semicolon**. Java uses the semicolon to know where the instruction stops.
blocks.caption: The broken version forgets the semicolon after println. Java points near the line where it got confused.
When Java gives a compiler error, read the first one first. Later errors are often just aftershocks from the first missing symbol.

sections.title: Braces, comments, and type checks
sections.summary: Trace how **braces** group code, **comments** disappear, and type mistakes stop compilation.

blocks.caption: Curly braces group statements into a **block**. The class opens one block, `main` opens another, and the `if` opens another. Lines inside the `if` braces run only when the condition is true.
blocks.output:
Nice work
Keep it up
Done

blocks.title: Braces decide the block, not the spaces
blocks.body: In Java, indentation helps people read. Braces control the program. If indentation and braces disagree, Java follows the braces.

choices: It fails to compile, because the last line is indented wrong
blocks.why: `score` is 50, so `score > 80` is false and "Nice work" is skipped. The last line is indented as though it belonged to the `if`, but the closing brace on the line above already shut that block. The line is part of `main`, not part of the `if`, so it prints for any score at all. If you picked "Nothing at all", you read the indentation the way Python trained you to. Java looks straight past it. Odd indentation is ugly, not illegal, so this compiles fine.

blocks.caption: Anything after `//` is a **comment**. A `/* ... */` comment can span multiple lines. Java is also **case sensitive**, so `System` and `system` are different names.

blocks.body: Java is **compiled before it runs**. The compiler reads the whole file and checks types first. If a line gives text to an `int`, the program does not start at all.

blocks.caption: This prints nothing because the file does not compile. Java sees a string being stored in an `int` and stops before any line runs.

blocks.prompt: This code is saved in a **file** named `Greeter.java`. Why does it fail to compile?
choices: Two reasons: the `println` statement has no semicolon, and the file name does not match the class name
Just the missing semicolon. The file name is up to you.
Just the file name. A `println` line does not need a semicolon.
blocks.why: Both rules are broken. `System.out.println("Hi")` is a statement, so it needs a semicolon. And a `public class Greeting` has to live in `Greeting.java`, while this **file** is called `Greeter.java`. Worth knowing: the compiler will not **list** both at once. It cannot finish reading a file it cannot parse, so it reports the missing semicolon and quits. Only after you add the semicolon and compile again does it get far enough to notice the name and tell you `class Greeting is public, should be declared in a file named Greeting.java`. Two errors, two rounds. That is the normal rhythm of fixing Java: repair the first complaint, compile, see what was hiding behind it.

sections.title: Use the compiler checklist
sections.summary: When Java refuses to compile, check the **first compiler message** and the small symbols around it.

blocks.title: What to check when Java refuses to compile
items: **Class** name and file name should match when the class is public.
Most statements end with a semicolon.
Read the first compiler error before changing five things.
